prompt: Why are the tests written in earlier lessons the project's best security checks?

choices.text: They run faster than any other tool
choices.why: Speed helps, and it is not the reason.

choices.text: They state what this application must refuse
choices.why: Right. No general tool can know that.

choices.text: They reach every line of code
choices.why: Coverage is not the point; refusals are.

choices.text: They replace code review
choices.why: They complement it; lesson 18 still applies.

prompt: A project has 95% line coverage and still ships lesson 1's flaw. How?

choices.text: Coverage tools miss Flask routes
choices.why: They count route lines like any others.

choices.text: The remaining 5% held the flaw
choices.why: The flawed lines can be covered; that is the trouble.

choices.text: Coverage counts lines that ran, not refusals asked for
choices.why: Right. A test of the happy path runs the cancel route and never asks whose booking it is.

choices.text: High coverage makes tests slower and less reliable
choices.why: Not the mechanism here.

prompt: Which make a security test worth keeping? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: it states a refusal
choices.why: The thing the application must not do.

choices.text: it uses the value that matters in its context
choices.why: Ordinary data passes every version.

choices.text: it checks that nothing changed after the refusal
choices.why: A status alone can hide a side effect.

choices.text: it is called test_cancel_2
choices.why: A name that reads as the requirement is better.

prompt: Match each tool to what it reads.

pairs.right: the source code, without running it

prompt: How many findings did bandit report for app.py alone?
Why does a password-reset code need `secrets` rather than `random`?

choices.text: random cannot produce digits
choices.why: It produces them happily.

choices.text: secrets produces longer codes
choices.why: The length is decided by the code, not the module.

choices.text: Its output is predictable
choices.why: Right. random is predictable from enough of its output; secrets draws from the operating system's secure source.

choices.text: random is removed in Python 3.13
choices.why: It is still there, for simulations.

prompt: Why did both tests pass while bandit found four problems?

choices.text: The return values never change
choices.why: Right. None of the four changes what the functions return; that is the gap a static check fills.

choices.text: The tests were run without the virtual environment
choices.why: They ran in it, and passed.

choices.text: bandit is wrong about all four
choices.why: Three are real problems and one is a stated exception.

choices.text: pytest skips functions that use hashlib
choices.why: It skips nothing.

prompt: What makes `app.run(debug=True)` dangerous outside a developer's own machine?

choices.text: It makes every page slower
choices.why: Speed is a minor effect.

choices.text: It disables the session cookie for the visitors of the site
choices.why: Sessions still work.

choices.text: It turns autoescaping off
choices.why: Escaping is unaffected.

choices.text: It runs Python from an error page
choices.why: Right. The PIN is printed in the server's log, and the page hands over the server.

prompt: bandit's identifier for a password written as a string in the code is B___.
bandit reports B101 on every assert in test_app.py. What is the right answer?

choices.text: Stop using assert in tests
choices.why: assert is how a pytest test states what it expects.

choices.text: Exclude the test files from the scan
choices.why: Right. One decision, made once, in the command everybody runs.

choices.text: Add a bare # nosec to each line
choices.why: A bare nosec silences future findings on the line too.

choices.text: Switch bandit off for the project
choices.why: That loses the four real findings with the noise.

prompt: The receipt id uses MD5 and protects nothing. How does the fixed code say so?

choices.text: It switches to SHA-256, which bandit never reports
choices.why: A different change, and not what the code says about intent.

choices.text: It removes the function
choices.why: The receipt still needs an id.

choices.text: usedforsecurity=False
choices.why: Right. The intention sits beside the line it explains.

choices.text: A comment at the top of the file
choices.why: Far from the line, and invisible to the tool.

prompt: Why is a bare `# nosec` worse than `# nosec B324: receipt ids are labels`?

choices.text: bandit refuses comments without a rule
choices.why: It accepts them, which is the problem.

choices.text: It silences future findings too
choices.why: Right. It silences every future finding on that line, with no reason; a real one added later passes unseen.

choices.text: It makes the scan slower
choices.why: No measurable effect.

choices.text: It works in test files and nowhere else
choices.why: It works anywhere.

prompt: Match each finding to the answer the lesson gives.

pairs.right: exclude those files from the scan

prompt: B201 has high severity and medium confidence. What does that combination say?

choices.text: The finding is probably false
choices.why: Medium confidence is not low.

choices.text: Bad if real; uncertain where it runs
choices.why: Right. Neither number is a verdict; they order the reading.

choices.text: It is to be fixed before any other finding
choices.why: The numbers order the reading, not the fixing.

choices.text: It only matters in production
choices.why: The code is the same everywhere; where it runs is the question.

prompt: What does `set -e` do in check.sh?

choices.text: It prints every command before running it
choices.why: That is set -x.

choices.text: It stops at the first command that fails
choices.why: Right, and the script returns the failure.

choices.text: It runs the commands in parallel
choices.why: They run in order.

choices.text: It sets environment variables
choices.why: Not what -e means.

prompt: After the refused commit, `git log` shows nothing to undo. Why?

choices.text: git deleted the commit after the failure
choices.why: There was never a commit to delete.

choices.text: The hook ran before the commit existed
choices.why: Right. The accepted one is the root commit.

choices.text: bandit reverted the working tree
choices.why: bandit only reads.

choices.text: pytest cleaned the repository
choices.why: pytest does not touch git.

prompt: Why is a local pre-commit hook a courtesy rather than the team's control?

choices.text: Hooks only run on Linux
choices.why: They run on any system git runs on.

choices.text: Hooks cannot run Python tools
choices.why: This one ran three.

choices.text: It is not committed, and --no-verify skips it
choices.why: Right. The control is the same script on a server, for every change.

choices.text: It runs after the push, too late to help
choices.why: It runs before the commit.

prompt: git runs the file .git/hooks/___ before it records a commit, and refuses the commit if it fails.
Put the steps of check.sh in the order they run.
items: bandit over the code, test files excluded

prompt: Which flaw do pytest, bandit and pip-audit all miss unless somebody wrote a test for it?

choices.text: random used for a reset code
choices.why: bandit reports it as B311.

choices.text: jinja2 pinned at 3.1.4
choices.why: pip-audit reports it.

choices.text: a missing owner check
choices.why: Right. A route that never checks whose data it serves: nothing in it is a risky call; the flaw is a line that is absent.

choices.text: debug=True in app.run
choices.why: bandit reports it as B201.

prompt: What does a DAST tool such as OWASP ZAP do that the three tools do not?

choices.text: It tests the running application
choices.why: Right. It sends requests and examines the answers, pointed at a copy of your own application, in a test environment.

choices.text: It reads the source code more carefully
choices.why: That is static analysis, bandit's kind.

choices.text: It lists advisories for dependencies
choices.why: That is pip-audit's job.

choices.text: It writes the missing tests
choices.why: Nobody writes those but you.

prompt: A team says: check.sh is green, so the release is secure. What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: Agreed, if the pipeline ran it too
choices.why: Where it ran does not change what it checks.

choices.text: Green means nothing at all
choices.why: It means a great deal, as a floor.

choices.text: Green is a floor, not a certificate
choices.why: Right. Known refusals, known patterns, known advisories. Above the floor is knowing which refusals the application owes.

choices.text: A penetration test is what can say that
choices.why: No single activity certifies security.

prompt: A colleague adds `# nosec` to silence B105 on `API_KEY = "sk-…"` so the hook lets the commit through. What do you say?

choices.text: Fine, as long as the comment names the rule
choices.why: The finding is real; naming the rule does not make it safe.

choices.text: The finding is real: move the key out of the code, as lesson 16 shows
choices.why: Right. nosec is for patterns used safely on purpose, not for real flaws.

choices.text: Use git commit --no-verify instead
choices.why: That skips every check, not just this one.

choices.text: Exclude app.py from the scan
choices.why: That hides the whole application from the tool.

prompt: Which of these does check.sh as written catch before a commit? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: a test that stopped passing
choices.why: pytest runs first.

choices.text: Flask's debugger switched on in app.py
choices.why: bandit reports B201.

choices.text: a pinned dependency with a published advisory
choices.why: pip-audit reports it.

choices.text: a missing owner check in a new route with no test
choices.why: No tool sees an absent line with no test asking for it.

prompt: Why does the lesson keep all the checks behind one command?

choices.text: Three commands do not fit in one terminal
choices.why: They can.

choices.text: bandit refuses to run on its own
choices.why: It ran on its own earlier.

choices.text: Laptop and server run the same thing
choices.why: Right. Moving it into a pipeline is one line of configuration.

choices.text: One command is faster than three
choices.why: It runs the same three.
